opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition is this: when a model reasons by verbalizing, by writing out a chain of thought, every intermediate step has to be squeezed through the bottleneck of the vocabulary. At each step the model has this very rich, high-dimensional hidden state, and then it has to collapse all of that into a single discrete token, pick one word, and then continue from there. A lot of information gets thrown away in that sampling step. The model might be entertaining several possibilities at once, it might have some uncertainty it would like to carry forward, and all of that gets flattened.

If instead you let the model think in its latent space, so you just keep iterating on the hidden state, recurring over it, without ever decoding to text, then in principle it can keep all of that information around. It can represent things that don't have a neat word attached to them. It can keep multiple hypotheses in superposition, so to speak, and refine them over many steps. That was part of the motivation behind our work on recurrent-depth models, where you have a block that you can loop as many times as you want at test time, and the model just gets more compute to think about a token without having to produce anything visible.

There's also an efficiency argument. Verbalized reasoning is expensive. You're generating long sequences, the context grows, and you need training data that actually demonstrates these reasoning traces, which is a strong assumption. With latent reasoning you don't need specialized chain-of-thought data. The model can learn during pretraining to make use of additional recurrence when a problem is harder, and you can scale up compute at test time just by iterating more, without blowing up the context window.

And then, I think there's a slightly more philosophical point. Not all of human thinking is verbal either. A lot of what we do, spatial reasoning, intuition, things like that, we don't really put into words, and it would be a bit surprising if the best way for a machine to think was strictly through language that was designed for communication, not computation. Language is great for communicating the result of your thinking, but it's not obviously the optimal medium for the thinking itself.

Now, to be fair, there are tradeoffs. You lose some interpretability, because you can't just read the chain of thought anymore, and that's a real concern. But from a pure capability standpoint, I think there's a good argument that thinking in continuous space is strictly more expressive than thinking in tokens, and that's why I find it really exciting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the chain-of-thought paradigm, where the model writes out its reasoning token by token, is really powerful, but it's also a bit of a strange constraint when you think about it. Every intermediate step of the computation has to be squeezed through this bottleneck of discrete tokens. The model has a very rich, high-dimensional internal state, and then at every step we force it to collapse that down to one word out of a vocabulary, and then it has to re-read that word and reconstruct the context from it. That's a lossy channel.

And the other thing is that language is just not the natural substrate for a lot of reasoning. If you think about how you yourself reason, a lot of it isn't verbal. When you're doing spatial reasoning, or you're planning a sequence of moves, or you have some intuition that something is wrong before you can say why, that's not happening in words. Words are what you produce at the end when you want to communicate it to someone else. So there's a bit of an open question of whether we're forcing the model into a mode that's really about communication rather than about computation.

So what we were interested in is: can you give the model more compute at test time, the same way chain-of-thought does, but let that compute happen in the latent space? So instead of generating more tokens, the model iterates on its own hidden state. It takes its internal representation, runs it back through a block of layers, refines it, and does that as many times as it needs before it commits to an output token. From the outside it's still a standard transformer that reads and writes text, but internally it's doing recurrent computation in a continuous space that was never forced to be verbalizable.

And there are a couple of reasons I think that's potentially more powerful. One is the capacity argument I mentioned: the hidden state carries far more information than a token does, so you're not throwing things away between steps. Another is that it's adaptive in a very natural way. Some tokens are easy and some are hard, and a model that can loop in latent space can spend more iterations on the hard ones without having to invent some verbal scaffolding to justify spending that time. And a third, which I find kind of interesting, is that you don't need the training data to contain examples of the reasoning. With chain-of-thought you're to some extent limited by whether people wrote down their thinking in text form, and for a lot of problem types nobody ever did. If the reasoning happens in latent space, the model can learn to use that compute from the outcome alone.

Now, I should say the obvious trade-off, which is interpretability. If the model's thinking is in words, you can at least read it, even if you're not sure it's faithful. If it's in a latent trajectory, you have to do actual work to figure out what's going on in there. So I don't think of this as a replacement for verbalized reasoning. I think of it as a different axis of scaling that we haven't really explored, and the question I'm most interested in is what happens when you have both: a model that can think quietly and then talk.

r001.rationale: The response describes looping over hidden states to add test-time computation, but it does not explain that a transformer's fixed number of layers limits computation depth for a single generated token.

astra-6.text:
Well, when we ask a language model to think out loud, we're asking it to do two things at once: solve the problem and express every intermediate step in language. And it's not obvious that language is the best representation for every intermediate computation.

Inside a transformer, you have these high-dimensional continuous representations. There’s room to represent information that would be difficult to capture in a single token. If you can keep computing in that space, you don’t have to keep translating the intermediate result into a word and then reading that word back in to continue.

For me, the interesting possibility is giving the model more computation without requiring more text. It could spend longer working on something internally and only produce an answer when it’s ready. That doesn’t automatically make it better—you still have to figure out how to train it to use that computation effectively—but it removes a constraint that we impose when we equate thinking with generating a longer chain of words.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you think about how we use these models to reason, we usually ask them to write out a chain of thought. And that means every intermediate step has to pass through this bottleneck of producing a token—a word or part of a word. But there’s no particular reason that the best representation for solving a problem should look like a sentence.

Inside the transformer, you have these high-dimensional continuous representations. Potentially, you can carry information there that’s much richer than what you can express in a single token. If you let the model keep computing in that space before it commits to an output, it could refine a hypothesis or work through a problem without having to translate every intermediate state into language.

The important caveat is that you have to teach it to use that extra computation. Simply running it for longer doesn’t automatically give you better reasoning. But it opens up the possibility of separating how much computation the model spends on a problem from how much text it produces.

r001.rationale: The response describes token-by-token chain-of-thought as a bottleneck and richer internal representations, but it does not explain that a fixed number of transformer layers limits computation depth when generating a single token.
